analysis.one_liner: Gives federal health officials authority to order mandatory recalls of dangerous drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to require any registered drug producer to notify the Secretary of Health and Human Services when it has reason to believe a drug is adulterated or misbranded and could cause serious harm or death [S2] [S3]. It would let the Secretary order distributors to immediately stop shipping the drug, hold an informal hearing within five days if the company appeals, and amend the order into a mandatory recall [S2] [S3]. In an emergency with credible evidence of an imminent threat, the Secretary could order an immediate recall that continues even while the appeal is pending [S2] [S3]. It would also require notice of recall orders to consumers and state and local health officials, and make failure to comply a violation of the Act [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and their families, who would learn faster when a drug on their shelf is contaminated, mislabeled, or otherwise dangerous, and who would be directly notified of a recall order. The bill specifically directs the Secretary to notify consumers to whom the drug was distributed [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients taking prescription and over-the-counter drugs

how_it_helps.text: Before this bill, the Secretary could only request a voluntary recall of a dangerous drug; the bill's own savings clause preserves that voluntary-request power, showing that mandatory authority was the gap it aimed to fill [S3].

The bill would require registered drug producers themselves to alert HHS as soon as practicable when they have reason to believe a drug is adulterated or misbranded and poses a reasonable probability of serious health consequences or death [S2] [S3].

The Secretary could order immediate cessation of distribution, upgrade that to a mandatory recall after a fast informal hearing, and issue an emergency recall that must proceed even while the company's 24-hour appeal is pending [S3].
Recall orders would trigger notice to consumers and to state and local health officials, closing the gap where people keep taking a dangerous drug because no one told them [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers and distributors, who would bear the cost of mandatory recalls, compliance reporting, and lost sales on products the government orders off the market [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The deadlines are tight by design: a company hit with a cease-distribution order gets only 24 hours to appeal and a hearing within about five days, which could force an error-free response on short notice from smaller firms [S3].

Mandatory recalls impose real costs on manufacturers — destroying inventory, refunding or replacing product, and running consumer notices — costs that would fall even on companies that dispute the government's finding [S3].
The bill covers drugs but not medical devices, leaving a parallel safety gap untouched even though devices were part of the committee's jurisdiction [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct: when a drug can seriously injure or kill, the difference between asking a company nicely and ordering it off the market is measured in patient exposure days. The costs — recall expenses and tight deadlines for companies — are real but are the ordinary price of a functioning safety system, and the bill keeps a due-process pathway with a prompt hearing and the possibility of vacating an order if grounds are inadequate [S3]. The design is lean but defensible.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again; the committee held no markup and the House never voted, so the bill died when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edolphus Towns introduced the bill on July 14, 2010, with four Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1] [S5].
That referral was the bill's last action; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended [S5].

The bill would have given the Secretary of Health and Human Services mandatory cease-distribution and recall authority over dangerous drugs, replacing a framework in which the Secretary could only request voluntary recalls [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers and distributors are better off, because the legal system under which the government can only request voluntary recalls of dangerous drugs — the framework this bill would have replaced — remained in place. Consumers gained nothing; the notification and mandatory recall protections never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers kept the voluntary-recall status quo

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create mandatory recall authority for adulterated or misbranded drugs.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only four Democratic cosponsors signed on and no Republican did, but no vote was ever held, so the record shows a thin Democratic-sponsored bill that died quietly rather than a party-line defeat.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed mandatory recall obligations, compliance reporting, and lost sales on dangerous products, replacing the voluntary-recall framework in which companies could negotiate with the Secretary instead of being ordered [S2] [S3]. Its interest in keeping recalls voluntary ran against the bill's consumer-notification and immediate-removal protections. Because the bill died, the industry kept the existing framework.
